messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 42
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Farmer
  trauma_type: Child's life-threatening illness
  pcl5: 76

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Visual (Body Parts): Specific body parts associated with the event, Nighttime/Dark: Night-time or waking up in the dark, Certain Songs: Certain songs
  Maladaptive Strategies: Delay Sleep: stay up until very late, Avoid People: avoid other people, Avoid Sleep: Going to sleep or lying in the dark
  Memory: Reliving Event: When I remember the frightening event I feel like it is happening right now., Sudden Pieces: Fragments of the memory appear suddenly without warning and then disappear, Feels Present Not Past: The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Sokha is a 42-year-old Cambodian American man who has spent most of his adult life working as a farmer, alongside his wife, on leased land where the days begin before sunrise and often end well after dark. When he speaks about why he has come for help now, he does not begin with himself. He begins with his son, and with a period several years ago when the boy became critically ill and was taken to the hospital with a condition Sokha understood at the time as life-threatening. What remains most vivid to him is not a single orderly story but flashes that seize him whole: his son’s small body in a hospital bed, the exposed parts of him that had to be examined and treated, the look of his skin under harsh lights, the sight of tubes and hands moving over him while Sokha stood by feeling useless. In his account, the nights are the worst part of the memory. He remembers being jolted awake in a dark hospital room, unable for a few seconds to place where he was, hearing monitors and low voices, and then seeing his child’s body again and feeling a rush of dread as if he were about to lose him.

Since that illness, Sokha says that remembering does not feel like remembering. He does not describe a distant event that he can revisit at will. Instead, pieces of it break into the present without warning. He can be walking through a field checking irrigation lines or sorting tools in the shed and suddenly a fragment is there—the sight of his son’s arm, the angle of his torso in the bed, a glimpse of skin that immediately takes him back. In those moments he feels as if the hospital scene is happening again now, not as something over and finished. He has difficulty putting the full sequence into words because it comes in disjointed pieces that flare up and vanish, leaving him shaken and irritable. What unsettles him most is how immediate it feels. He knows intellectually that his son survived, but when the memory arrives, that knowledge does not seem to belong to the same moment.

His triggers have become woven into the ordinary texture of his life. Nighttime is especially difficult. On the farm, darkness means the workday is done and the house has gone quiet, and this is exactly when he becomes tense. Waking in the dark is worse. If he opens his eyes and the room is unlit, there is a split second in which he feels he is back in that hospital night, bracing himself to look toward the bed. He has gradually begun staying up very late, sometimes sitting in the kitchen or outside with a light on, telling himself he is not tired or that there is still something to repair for the next day. Going to bed, lying down, and being in the dark feel dangerous in a way he cannot easily explain to his wife except to say that his mind becomes “too open.” Certain songs also catch him off guard. If one comes on the radio in the truck or is playing in a market or at a family gathering, he stiffens and goes quiet. He connects them to that period around his son’s illness, and once he hears them he is no longer fully in the present.

Over the months and years, Sokha has made his world smaller. He avoids people more than he used to, passing up visits, lingering less at community gatherings, and keeping conversations brief even with relatives. He prefers to stay occupied with work he can do alone, where he does not have to risk a song coming on in the background or explain why he suddenly looks distracted. On the farm this has had practical consequences. Farming is physical, early, and communal at certain points in the season, but because he stays up so late, he starts some mornings already worn down. He has become less available to neighbors and extended family who once could count on him, and his wife has noticed that he withdraws when evenings should be family time. He is not describing a loss of love for them; rather, he seems convinced that being around others makes it harder to control what might intrude on him.

By the time he sought help, Sokha felt trapped by a routine built around outrunning the dark and the moment of sleep. He had recently woken abruptly before dawn, in a dark room, with the full force of the hospital experience on him again, and for several moments he could not orient himself to his own house. That episode frightened him enough that he could no longer dismiss this as simple stress. He says he wants to be able to sleep like a normal person and to be with his family in the evening without scanning for what might set him off. What frightens him most is not only the return of the memory itself, but the way it takes over so completely that the past no longer feels past.
